lessons.title: Exchange rates and the rupee
lessons.summary: What USD/LKR means and who publishes it.

cards.title: A price for money
cards.body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. USD/LKR at 300 means one US dollar costs Rs 300.

cards.title: CBSL's daily rates
cards.body: Every business day the Central Bank of Sri Lanka publishes indicative rates for about 55 currencies, worked out each morning from the USD/LKR market rate and world currency prices. The trainer's live prices use them.

cards.title: Weaker or stronger
cards.body: If USD/LKR rises from 300 to 310, each dollar costs more rupees: the rupee has weakened. Imports like fuel and medicine get dearer, and anyone holding dollars has more rupees' worth.

cards.title: Not just dollars
cards.body: Rates move for every currency. Families receiving money from relatives in the Middle East, Europe or Australia feel these moves directly.

quiz.question: USD/LKR moves from 300 to 310. What happened to the rupee?
quiz.explanation: Each dollar now costs Rs 10 more, so the rupee buys less: it weakened.

quiz.question: Who publishes the daily indicative exchange rates in Sri Lanka?
options: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka
quiz.explanation: The Central Bank of Sri Lanka publishes them every business day.

quiz.question: You hold US$100 and the rupee weakens. In rupees, your dollars are worth…
quiz.explanation: Each dollar now converts into more rupees.

lessons.title: Buying and selling rates
lessons.summary: Why you lose a little every time you swap.

cards.title: Two prices
cards.body: Banks sell you foreign currency at a higher selling rate and buy it back at a lower buying rate. The gap is the spread, and it's how they earn.

cards.title: The trainer's spread
cards.body: In the trainer you buy at the CBSL rate plus 0.75% and sell at it minus 0.75%: a 1.5% round trip. Cash notes usually have wider spreads than bank transfers.

cards.title: Start behind
cards.body: Buy and sell straight back and you lose the spread. The currency has to move in your favour by more than that before you make anything.

quiz.question: What is the spread?
options: The gap between the bank's buying and selling rates
Interest on a foreign currency account
quiz.explanation: Banks sell high and buy low; the difference is the spread.

quiz.question: With a 1.5% round-trip spread, roughly how much do you lose buying Rs 100,000 of dollars and selling them straight back?
Which usually has the wider spread?
quiz.explanation: Handling cash costs banks more, so cash rates are usually worse.

lessons.title: Currency risk
lessons.summary: Rupees can fall fast — and recover.

cards.title: Big moves happen
cards.body: In 2022 the rupee lost over 40% of its value against the dollar in a few months. In 2023 it won back part of that. Currencies can move both ways.

cards.title: No interest by itself
cards.body: Notes in a drawer earn nothing. A foreign currency deposit earns interest, usually less than rupee FDs. Your return depends mostly on the exchange rate.

cards.title: Rules apply
cards.body: Banks offer foreign currency accounts, but who can open them and how the money can be used is set under Sri Lanka's Foreign Exchange Act. Ask your bank before you buy.

cards.title: A hedge, not a bet
cards.body: Holding some foreign currency can protect you if you'll need it later — for study, travel or imports. Buying it hoping for a quick profit is speculation.

quiz.question: Can the rupee strengthen after a big fall?
options: Yes — it won back part of its fall in 2023
quiz.explanation: Currencies move both ways; after falling sharply in 2022 the rupee recovered some ground in 2023.

quiz.question: Foreign currency notes kept at home earn…
quiz.explanation: Cash earns nothing; only the exchange rate can change its rupee value.

quiz.question: When does holding foreign currency make the most sense?
options: When you'll need that currency later
Whenever you want a quick profit
Only when the rupee is strong
quiz.explanation: Matching currency to a future need (study, travel, imports) removes exchange-rate risk for that need.
